title: Indexes and B-trees

answers: Yes, every database forbids using a non-leading index column
No; index and skip-scan choices depend on the database and data, so inspect EXPLAIN
The column names alone guarantee that the index will be chosen
writing.exampleCaption: Inspect EXPLAIN with representative data. An absent leading-column filter does not universally prohibit an index scan.
writing.explanation:
A selective B-tree index can reduce work by narrowing the scanned range. Leading-column predicates are often especially useful, but they are not a universal eligibility rule: PostgreSQL can use later-column constraints and skip scans when its planner estimates that they are worthwhile. Every maintained index also adds storage and write work; measure those costs rather than declaring a table slow from its index count alone.

An index is another data structure maintained alongside table rows so some queries can avoid examining every row. A B-tree-family index commonly supports equality, range scans, and ordered traversal. For a composite index on `(account_id, created_at)`, queries restricted by account can often use the leading part, and a query for one account ordered by time can benefit from the second part. A query only on `created_at` may not use the index efficiently, though optimizers and specialized access paths vary by database.

Indexes cost storage and write work. Each insert or update that changes an indexed field may need to modify the index. An index on a low-selectivity column can be less useful than it looks, and a query planner may choose a scan for a small table. Do not add an index solely because a WHERE clause exists. Inspect the actual query plan and measure it with representative row counts and distributions.

For an interview, start from a concrete query and data shape. Explain which predicate narrows the search, whether the requested columns are covered, and whether an ordered scan avoids a separate sort. Then state the cost to writes and memory. Test after adding the index: plans can change as statistics and data grow. The leftmost-prefix heuristic is useful, but a real planner makes the final decision.

A covering index may avoid fetching full table rows when it contains every value a query needs. That can be faster for a frequent narrow query but makes the index larger and more expensive to maintain. Discuss cardinality and selectivity with real data: an index useful on a huge selective table may do little on a tiny table.
writing.feedback: PostgreSQL documents multicolumn B-tree skip scans and later-column restrictions. A leading predicate is often useful, but index eligibility and planner choice are different questions.

writing.question: Can the index (tenant_id, kind, at) be ruled out solely because tenant_id is not filtered?

writing.summary: An index is a sorted structure that trades write cost for read speed.
writing.task: Use EXPLAIN on both a leading-column query and a later-column query in the named database. Compare selectivity, data distribution and actual plans instead of predicting a universal yes or no.
